About us

Stats NZ Tatauranga Aotearoa supplies some of New Zealand’s most important statistics, data and insights to allow decision makers to make informed decisions to improve social, economic and environmental growth for New Zealanders. We are the source of official statistics and the leader of the Official Statistics System and of New Zealand’s public sector data and analytics system. Stats NZ collects and releases information on a wide range of subjects including population, businesses, the economy, people and communities, and industry. Contact our Information Centre for help finding information and data on our website, or for guidance on how to use our online tools. Call toll-free on 0508 525 525 or email info@stats.govt.nz. You can also follow us on Twitter @Stats_NZ. Terms of use for Stats NZ LinkedIn accounts: http://ow.ly/ACop309OZy7

    Stats NZ is focussed on modernising New Zealand’s official economic statistics, providing more frequent and accurate information about the economy. A key part of this work is providing the Consumers Price Index monthly as well as quarterly from 2027. The move will give New Zealanders access to more frequent information about changing prices, helping households, businesses and government make better-informed decisions. “Providing a monthly CPI represents a major change to one of New Zealand’s most important economic measures, so it is essential this is done with quality and trust at its heart,’’ says Government Statistician and Stats NZ Chief Executive Colin Lynch. Today, we announced the pathway for delivering the new monthly CPI. The monthly CPI will be introduced in stages, with transitional reports in May and June 2027 to give customers an opportunity to work with the monthly data before ongoing publication begins from July 2027. The transitional phases will give data users the opportunity to test how the data works with their systems, how they access it, and how they interpret and use monthly price movements. “It will help them prepare their systems and analysis, provide feedback to us, and build confidence in how the monthly data should be used,” says Colin. “This is not simply a matter of publishing the existing CPI more often,” he says. “We are changing how price information is collected, processed, checked and published so we can produce reliable information every month.” The currently quarterly CPI releases will continue alongside the new monthly releases to provide continuity for users.

    We’re pleased to announce some updates and improvements to the Place and Ethnic Group Summaries tool on our website. The tool is a free online service providing data about New Zealand’s communities and ethnic groups. Topics include population, work, income, education, and housing. The Place and Ethnic Group Summaries data is updated every six months. Another year of data has been recently added for births and deaths; building consents; unemployment, under-utilisation and labour force participation rates; life satisfaction and child poverty. In response to customer requests, the tool now also shows counts alongside percentages in most graphs and tables – handy!

    Quality is at the heart of everything we do at Stats NZ. We’re committed to continually improving how we produce and share data, and to being open about the systems behind it. To do this we have published our statistical quality assurance system, which is our framework to guide quality. Read more in Gary’s post below 👇

    Gary Dunnet
    1mo

    Quality is at the heart of our work at Stats NZ (& for that matter any NSO).   It’s our job to provide data and insights that people can trust. Communities, businesses, and governments rely on the data and statistics produced by Stats NZ when making important decisions that affect New Zealanders, every day.   Quality matters at every stage of the process. Our statistical quality assurance system combines international best practice with what works in a New Zealand context.   The system has six parts that cover everything from making sure we understand what’s needed, through to publication, and on into the future. Each part works together and cover: Statistical design, Data and IT system controls, Quality assurance processes, Documentation, Governance and accountability, and Culture and capability.   This system shows what ‘good’ looks like and will be used to improve existing processes and guide new ones.   It can also be used as a framework to help identify where change is needed. For example, it was used in early 2026 to review an error with the Food Price Index and identify areas for improvement.   So that interested people can understand more about the way we work, we have published a paper with more detailed information about the system. Find the paper here: https://lnkd.in/ewa8BeFB. #statsnz #NSO #qualitymeasurement

    Last week, we welcomed officials from the Government Data Division of Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information to our Wellington offices ahead of the NZ Gov Data Summit. Joined by colleagues from the Government Digital Delivery Agency, we had a discussion on data stewardship and digital government. The conversation covered the similarities and differences between Singapore’s centralised data system and New Zealand’s distributed model, approaches to data governance, and ways to build public understanding and trust around how governments use data. The delegation was particularly interested in our experience supporting agencies to assess and lift their data maturity, as Singapore looks to adopt a diagnostic tool of its own.  The NZ Gov Data Summit brought together more than 200 senior leaders, policymakers, and technology experts. Senior leaders from Stats NZ were in attendance, including Graeme Simpson (Chief Technology Officer), who spoke on a leadership panel exploring what it will take to future‑proof Aotearoa’s digital capabilities and strengthen citizen trust through the ethical and transparent use of data and AI. Engagements like these are a valuable opportunity to exchange perspectives, learn from different system approaches, and strengthen relationships across the global public service community. We look forward to continuing the dialogue and sharing knowledge as we work towards trusted, people‑centred digital government.
